case_overview.case_name: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru and Ors. v. State of Kerala and Anr.
case_overview.parties: Petitioner: His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru and Ors. | Respondent: State of Kerala and Anr.
case_overview.bench: S.M. Sikri, C.J., A.N. Grover, A.N. Ray, D.G. Palekar, H.R. Khanna, J.M. Shelat, K.K. Mathew, K.S. Hegde, M.H. Beg, P. Jaganmohan Reddy, S.N. Dwivedi, Y.V. Chandrachud, JJ.

facts_of_case.point: The petitioner filed Writ Petition No. 135 of 1970 on March 21, 1970 under Article 32 of the Constitution for enforcement of fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 25, 26, and 31.

The petitioner challenged the Constitutional validity of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 (Act 1 of 1964) as amended by the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969 (Act 35 of 1969). The Supreme Court issued a rule nisi on March 25, 1970.

During the pendency of the writ petition, the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1971 (Kerala Act No. 25 of 1971) was passed and received the assent of the President on August 7, 1971, leading the petitioner to seek leave to challenge it as well.

While the matter was pending, Parliament passed the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971, the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971, and the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972, which were subsequently challenged by the petitioner.

legal_issues.issue: What is the scope, ambit, and extent of the amending power conferred on Parliament under Article 368 of the Constitution?
Whether the amending power under Article 368 is subject to express limitations under Article 13(2) or implied and inherent limitations.
Whether Parliament under Article 368 has the power to alter, destroy, or abrogate the essential features or basic structure of the Constitution.
Whether the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971, the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971, and the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 are Constitutionally valid.

important_arguments_or_content.point: The petitioners contended that the amending power of Parliament under Article 368 is limited and does not extend to destroying or altering the essential features, basic elements, and fundamental principles of the Constitution.
The petitioners argued that Fundamental Rights form an essential feature of the Constitution and cannot be abrogated or taken away through Constitutional amendments.

The respondents claimed that the amending body under Article 368 possesses unlimited constituent power, allowing Parliament to amend, alter, or repeal any provision of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, provided procedural requirements are met.

The petitioners challenged Article 31C (introduced by the 25th Amendment), arguing it delegates constituent amending power to State Legislatures, destroys judicial review, and subverts fundamental freedoms.

court_reasoning.point: The Court held that the power to amend the Constitution resides in Article 368 itself and is an exercise of constituent power, not ordinary legislative power under residuary entry 97 of List I.
The term 'law' in Article 13(2) refers to ordinary legislative laws and does not apply to Constitutional amendments made under Article 368.

The majority of the Bench reasoned that while the amending power under Article 368 is wide, the word 'amendment' carries implied limitations and does not enable Parliament to alter or destroy the basic structure or essential framework of the Constitution.

Regarding Section 2 of the 25th Amendment, replacing 'compensation' with 'amount' in Article 31(2) excludes judicial review on the adequacy of the amount, provided the amount is not illusory or arbitrary and principles specified are relevant.

Regarding Section 3 of the 25th Amendment (Article 31C), the second part excluding judicial review by way of a declaration was held invalid as it deprives courts of checking whether a law actually gives effect to Directive Principles, thereby affecting the basic structure.

decision_or_conclusion.point: The Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971 was held to be Constitutionally valid.
Section 2 of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971 was upheld as valid.

Section 3 of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971 (Article 31C) was declared unconstitutional/invalid in part—specifically the clause barring judicial review via a declaration—while the remaining part was upheld subject to judicial scrutiny of the nexus to Directive Principles.
The Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 was declared valid, leaving the validity of the specific Acts included in the Ninth Schedule to be determined by the Constitution Bench.
The cases were remitted to the Constitution Bench for final disposal in accordance with the judgment and the law.

important_legal_provisions.context: Governs the power and procedure for amending the Constitution.
Prohibits the State from making laws that take away or abridge fundamental rights.
Relates to compulsory acquisition or requisitioning of property and payment of an 'amount'.
Protects laws giving effect to Directive Principles in Article 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14, 19, and 31.
Saves specific Acts and Regulations added to the Ninth Schedule from being invalidated for violating Part III rights.

summary.simplified_explanation: This landmark case addressed whether Parliament has unlimited power to change the Indian Constitution. A religious leader in Kerala challenged state land reform laws that affected his monastery's property. During the case, Parliament passed Constitutional amendments (24th, 25th, and 29th Amendments) to give itself broader powers to amend the Constitution and limit court challenges to land reform laws. The Supreme Court decided that while Parliament has wide powers to amend any part of the Constitution, including fundamental rights, it cannot change or destroy the 'basic structure' or foundational features of the Constitution. The Court upheld Parliament's power to amend the Constitution (24th Amendment) but struck down the portion of Article 31C that completely cut off the courts' power to review whether laws actually served public welfare objectives.
